whatIsFiber.question: What is fiber and why does it matter?
whatIsFiber.answer: Fiber is the part of plant foods (vegetables, legumes, whole grains, fruit) your body can't digest. It helps digestion stay regular and supports a balanced diet. Niébé, lentils, okra, fonio, and fruit are good Senegalese sources.

saltVsSodium.question: What's the difference between salt and sodium?
saltVsSodium.answer: Sodium is a mineral; table salt is roughly 40% sodium by weight. Nutrition guidance is often given in sodium (mg), while the salt you add at home is measured in grams — LifeOS shows both so the numbers stay clear.

whatIsFreeSugar.question: What is "free sugar"?
whatIsFreeSugar.answer: Free sugar is sugar added to food or drinks (like sugar stirred into tea, bissap, lakh, or thiakry) — not the natural sugar found inside whole fruit. Reducing free sugar means using less added sugar, not avoiding fruit.

howMuchSalt.question: How much salt is generally recommended?
howMuchSalt.answer: The World Health Organization recommends less than 5 grams of salt per day (about one teaspoon) for general health. This is general population guidance, not a personal medical prescription — see a clinician for advice specific to you.

reduceSodiumSenegalese.question: How can I reduce sodium in Senegalese cooking?
reduceSodiumSenegalese.answer: Use less bouillon cube per pot, build flavor with onion, garlic, ginger, citrus, and fresh herbs instead of extra salt, rinse salted or dried fish before cooking, and add salt at the table in small amounts rather than heavily salting during cooking.

balanceTraditionalMeals.question: Can I still eat traditional meals?
balanceTraditionalMeals.answer: Yes. The goal isn't to give up ceebu jën, mafé, or yassa — it's small adjustments (less oil, less bouillon, more vegetables, smaller starch portions) that keep the dishes you know while making the overall pattern more balanced.

whyVegetables.question: Why prioritize vegetables?
whyVegetables.answer: Vegetables add fiber, vitamins, and volume to a meal without much sodium or added sugar, which supports a generally balanced eating pattern.

whyWholeGrains.question: Why choose whole grains when possible?
whyWholeGrains.answer: Whole grains (like fonio, millet, or whole-grain bread) keep more of the grain's natural fiber compared to refined versions, which supports more balanced digestion.

whatIsLiverConscious.question: What does "liver-conscious" mean on LifeOS?
whatIsLiverConscious.answer: It means favoring generally balanced eating patterns — moderate sodium, limited added sugar, less fried/oily food, more vegetables and fiber, and little to no alcohol. It is general nutrition education, not a medical treatment for any liver condition.

hepatitisB.title: Hepatitis B & Nutrition
hepatitisB.intro: There is no special diet that treats, cures, removes, or controls hepatitis B. Diet does not replace medical care, monitoring, or treatment.
hepatitisB.focus: General liver-conscious eating focuses on an overall balanced pattern: moderate sodium, limited added sugar, less fried or oily food, more vegetables and fiber, and little to no alcohol — the same balanced-eating principles reflected throughout this Nutrition section.
hepatitisB.individualizedAdvice: Nutrition needs vary by individual, especially with other conditions like diabetes, kidney disease, hypertension, or pregnancy. Always follow the personalized guidance of your doctor or a registered dietitian.

fruitJuice.body: Fruit juice can contain substantial free sugar even when it has no added sugar — it isn't nutritionally identical to whole fruit.
fruitJuice.recommendation: Choose whole fruit more often than juice.

liverDetoxWarning.title: Be careful with "liver detox" drinks
liverDetoxWarning.body: There is no need for detox drinks as a treatment for hepatitis B. LifeOS does not recommend herbal products or supplements as hepatitis B treatment, and no drink — lemon water, ginger, bissap, baobab, or tea — cleanses or repairs the liver.

howMuchShouldIDrink.question: How much should I drink?
howMuchShouldIDrink.answer: Fluid needs vary by body size, age, activity level, climate, diet, pregnancy/breastfeeding, illness, medications, and kidney/heart conditions. A general adult starting range is about 2.0-2.5 L/day from fluids — a general estimate, not a personal prescription.

litersVsFluidOunces.question: Liters vs fluid ounces?
litersVsFluidOunces.answer: 1 L is about 34 fl oz. LifeOS shows both so you can use whichever unit is familiar to you.

whatCountsAsAFluid.question: What counts as a fluid?
whatCountsAsAFluid.answer: Water, sparkling water, unsweetened tea, coffee, and other non-alcoholic beverages all count. Alcoholic drinks are not counted toward hydration.

doesFoodProvideWater.question: Does food provide water?
doesFoodProvideWater.answer: Yes — fruits, vegetables, and soups contain water and contribute to overall fluid intake, though LifeOS's tracker here only counts drinks.

howCanIDrinkMoreWater.question: How can I drink more water?
howCanIDrinkMoreWater.answer: Keep water visible and within reach, add a slice of lemon or lime for flavor, and pair a glass of water with meals or habits you already have.

areSugaryDrinksGoodForHydration.question: Are sugary drinks good for hydration?
areSugaryDrinksGoodForHydration.answer: They can hydrate, but they add substantial free sugar without much nutritional value — water and unsweetened drinks are better everyday choices.

isFruitJuiceTheSameAsWholeFruit.question: Is fruit juice the same as whole fruit?
isFruitJuiceTheSameAsWholeFruit.answer: No. Fruit juice can contain substantial free sugar even without added sugar, and lacks the fiber of whole fruit. Choose whole fruit more often.

whatDrinksFitLiverConscious.question: What drinks fit a liver-conscious eating pattern?
whatDrinksFitLiverConscious.answer: Water, unsweetened sparkling water, unsweetened tea, and reduced-sugar traditional drinks fit well. Sugary drinks and alcohol are the main ones to limit.

shouldIDrinkMoreExercisingHeat.question: Should I drink more when exercising or in hot weather?
shouldIDrinkMoreExercisingHeat.answer: Often yes — activity and heat increase fluid loss. This is general guidance; ask your healthcare professional for advice specific to you, especially with a medical condition.
